questions.stem: Which statement about radioactive decay is true?

options.text: the timing of a single nucleus’s decay cannot be predicted
options.explanation: Decay is a random process — no prediction is possible for one nucleus.

options.text: scientists can predict when each nucleus will decay
options.explanation: Randomness forbids per-nucleus prediction.

options.text: decay happens only in artificial sources
options.explanation: Unstable nuclei decay wherever they are, natural or not.

options.text: decay always emits all three radiations at once
options.explanation: A given decay emits one type (or a subset), not necessarily all three.

questions.stem: What causes a nucleus to be unstable?

options.explanation: Decay needs no external light — it is spontaneous.

options.text: an imbalance of protons or neutrons
options.explanation: The proton-neutron balance is what the nucleus is sensitive to.
Electrons do not destabilise the nucleus.
Nuclear stability is unrelated to the atomic radius.

questions.stem: Why is carbon-14 unstable while carbon-12 is stable?

options.explanation: Stability is not about ionisation.
Electron count is irrelevant to nuclear stability.
The two additional neutrons unbalance the nucleus.
Both carbon isotopes have 6 protons.

questions.stem: What happens to a nucleus when it emits radiation?

options.explanation: Decay is the route towards stability.
The nucleus remains, transformed.
Emission, not absorption, defines decay.
The emission carries energy away, settling the nucleus.

questions.stem: Radiation from a decaying nucleus can be…

options.text: a high-energy particle or a high-energy wave
options.explanation: Alpha and beta are particles; gamma is a wave of the electromagnetic kind.
Gamma rays are waves, not particles.
Alpha and beta are particles.
The emissions are subatomic, not whole atoms.

questions.stem: Name the three types of radiation emitted from unstable nuclei.
questions.modelAnswer: The three emissions are alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
Radioactive decay is the process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation — a particle or wave — and becomes more stable.

questions.stem: Explain why it is impossible to state the moment when one particular unstable nucleus will decay.
questions.modelAnswer: Radioactive decay is a random process: each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in any interval, but nothing about its history or surroundings marks the exact moment.

questions.stem: A student claims carbon-14 should be stable because it is carbon. Use the proton-neutron story to correct them.
questions.modelAnswer: Being carbon fixes 6 protons but not stability; carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, two more than the stable carbon-12, and that proton-neutron imbalance makes its nucleus unstable.

questions.stem: What is an alpha particle identical to?

options.explanation: That is gamma radiation.
Alpha = 2 protons + 2 neutrons, the helium nucleus.
Hydrogen has one proton — not the alpha composition.
That is a beta particle.

options.text: a few centimetres of air only
options.explanation: Beta travels tens of centimetres in air.
Aluminium stops beta readily.
Beta is stopped by several millimetres of aluminium.
Paper stops alpha; beta sails through.

questions.stem: Which radiation has the greatest ionising power?

options.explanation: Beta ionises moderately.
Gamma is the weakest ioniser.
The three differ sharply in ionising ability.
Alpha is the most strongly ionising of the three.

questions.stem: Gamma rays are best described as…

options.explanation: Gamma is wave radiation with no mass or charge.
That is alpha.
Neutron emission is a separate, rarer decay mode.
Beta electrons are fast, and gamma is not an electron at all.

questions.stem: A source’s count rate falls sharply behind 5 mm of aluminium but barely changes behind paper or 5 mm of lead. Which radiation is emitted?

options.explanation: The paper result already rules alpha out.
Aluminium absorption identifies beta; paper and lead transparency exclude alpha and significant gamma.
Alpha would have been stopped by the paper.
Gamma would pass aluminium and be cut by thick lead.

questions.stem: State what a beta particle is and how it is produced inside a nucleus.
questions.modelAnswer: A beta particle is a high-energy electron, produced when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron.

questions.stem: Give the absorber that stops each of alpha, beta and gamma.
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by several centimetres of lead.

questions.stem: Explain why gamma is the most penetrating of the three radiations even though it is the weakest ioniser.
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma photons carry no charge and no mass, so they interact with matter only rarely; each interaction loses little energy, letting gamma travel far, while its weak interaction is also why it ionises least.

questions.stem: Count rates behind absorbers are: bare 4320, paper 4318, 5 mm aluminium 256, 5 mm lead 244. Identify the radiation and justify each step.
questions.modelAnswer: Paper barely changes the count (4320 → 4318), so no alpha; aluminium cuts it sharply (4320 → 256), so beta is present; lead leaves a similar residual (244), so no significant gamma. The source emits beta.
